title: Agentic AI’s Advantage for Health Insurers: Faster Decisions, Lower Costs, Better Care
gist: BCG argues health insurers face a demographic cliff — 30%–50% of experienced staff retiring within a decade — just as claim volumes and costs rise, and that agentic AI is the only remaining lever because classic efficiency plays (offshoring, RPA, service centers) have hit diminishing returns. Concrete payer deployments show 60%–80% of claims reimbursement automated, end-to-end claim time cut from 30–60 minutes to 2–4 minutes, and claims leakage down 3%–5% of total payout. The binding constraint is organizational, not technical: BCG's 10-20-70 rule puts 70% of the work in people, org, and process.

insights.claim: Health insurers will lose 30% to 50% of their experienced workforce to retirement over the next decade, with customer-facing and operations roles hit disproportionately hard.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Payer labor capacity shrinks on a known clock regardless of AI adoption, making automation spend non-discretionary rather than a margin-optimization choice — watch payer headcount and SG&A guidance for the crossover.
insights.quote: many payers will lose 30% to 50% of their experienced workforce to retirement over the next decade, with customer-facing and operations roles disproportionately affected
insights.locator: A Quietly Developing Crisis—and a Big Opportunity

insights.claim: The threat to health insurers is twofold — a structural inability to meet growing demand, and rising costs eroding margins and the ability to improve care — not merely a productivity problem.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Frames payer AI spend as capacity-preservation plus margin defense, meaning the ROI case survives even if cost savings underdeliver.
insights.locator: The threat is twofold

insights.claim: Personnel expense dominates spending in health insurance administration, and most of that administrative effort is concentrated in manual claims processing, enrollment, and benefit verification.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Identifies exactly which cost line agentic AI attacks — labor in three specific back-office processes — so automation announcements can be sized against payers' disclosed admin expense.
insights.locator: Personnel expense (which includes things like benefits) dominates

insights.claim: Case volumes and costs are rising from four compounding drivers — aging populations, growing chronic disease burden, costly innovation in medical treatments, and demand for new benefit types — while private insurance demand grows as it augments or replaces public-sector programs.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Volume growth for private payers is structurally driven, not cyclical — a tailwind for revenue but a squeeze on cost-to-serve unless unit processing cost falls.
insights.locator: Case volumes and associated costs are rising due to aging populations

insights.claim: Incremental gains from the classic health-insurer efficiency playbook — specialized service centers, customer service centers, rule-based process automation, outsourcing, and offshore processing — are now diminishing.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Bearish read-through for health-insurance BPO and offshore processing vendors whose growth depends on payers still having runway on the old levers.
insights.locator: The incremental gains from classic efficiency levers

insights.claim: Rule-based automation only works on predictable, fully structured processes, but most insurance workflows involve judgment, unstructured information, and exceptions — leaving payers with a patchwork of automation islands throttled by persistent manual chokepoints.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Explains why prior payer automation capex produced disappointing end-to-end results and why LLM-based agents are a category change rather than an incremental upgrade to RPA.
insights.quote: many payers have a patchwork of automation islands whose effectiveness is constrained by persistent manual chokepoints
insights.locator: Agents to the Rescue

insights.claim: Agentic AI shifts the strategic question from how to automate more steps to how to automate entire functions including multi-format inputs, i.e. from step-level to process-level automation.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: A useful diligence test for vendor claims: point tools that automate steps command far less value than platforms that own a whole process.
insights.quote: Agentic AI enables a shift from step-level automation to process-level automation.
insights.locator: As companies progress through the three phases

insights.claim: There are three tiers of agentic AI transformation — deploy off-the-shelf tools in everyday tasks, reshape critical functions, and invent new products and services — with sharply different payoffs.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: A grading rubric for payer AI disclosures: 'we rolled out copilots' is the lowest-value tier and should not be priced like a business-model change.
insights.locator: There are three approaches to agentic AI transformation

insights.claim: Off-the-shelf AI tools such as note-taking assistants, document summarization, and knowledge retrieval deliver typical gains of only 10% to 20% per employee, and those results are scattered and uneven.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Caps the realistic earnings impact of generic copilot seat licenses and argues per-seat AI vendors capture less enterprise value than workflow-owning platforms.
insights.quote: Typical gains are 10% to 20% per employee, but these results are scattered and uneven.
insights.locator: Most insurers are already deploying AI tools

insights.claim: Reorganizing processes into end-to-end agentic workflows yields efficiency gains of 30% to 80% depending on the starting point — three to four times the per-employee gains from off-the-shelf tools.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: The spread between 10%–20% and 30%–80% is the actual alpha in enterprise AI — favor companies restructuring processes over those buying tools.
insights.locator: In the reshape approach, companies reorganize processes

insights.claim: Eighty percent of leading companies concentrate their AI investments in the reshape and invent approaches rather than in scattered off-the-shelf tool deployment.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: A concrete benchmark for judging whether a company's AI budget mix resembles leaders or laggards.
insights.quote: Eighty percent of leading companies concentrate their AI investments in the reshape and invent approaches.
insights.locator: As companies progress through the three phases

insights.claim: Claims reimbursement and member enrollment/eligibility are each 60% to 80% automatable with agents handling intake, classification, unstructured data extraction, eligibility checks, duplicate detection, and decision proposals, with humans retained for rejections and disputes.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: These two processes are the highest-ceiling, most reusable targets — the first places to look for real payer cost takeout, and where automation vendors will compete hardest.
insights.locator: Claims Reimbursement. Agents take over managing document intake

insights.claim: Care approvals are only 40% to 60% automatable and fraud, waste, and abuse investigation 40% to 70%, materially lower ceilings than claims or enrollment because medical judgment, appeals, and provider negotiation stay human.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic upper bound on prior-authorization automation claims — vendors promising near-full automation of care approvals are over-promising against BCG's field data.
insights.locator: Care Approvals. Between 40% and 60% of this process

insights.claim: Benefits administration is 60% to 70% automatable, with agents calculating entitlement, determining payment triggers, detecting duplicates and fraud, and handling member communication while humans keep audit sampling, governance oversight, and policy updates.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Even in the highest-automation processes the residual human layer is audit and governance, meaning payer headcount reduction is partial and shifts cost from processing to controls.
insights.locator: Benefits Administration. Agents handle calculating benefit entitlement

insights.claim: In fraud detection, agents move beyond flagging by consolidating each patient's claims history by pathology and benchmarking treatment pathways against clinical guidelines, then ranking each anomaly by certainty and value.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Ranking by certainty AND recoverable value is the mechanism that turns fraud analytics into P&L impact — a differentiator to probe in payer-integrity vendor diligence.
insights.locator: Fraud, Waste, and Abuse Detection. Agents manage document collection

insights.claim: At a major European insurer, agentic AI cut end-to-end claim-processing time from 30–60 minutes to 2–4 minutes, roughly a 15x speedup on the core reimbursement workflow.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: A concrete magnitude to anchor payer automation forecasts, and a service-level weapon: cycle-time collapse is visible to members and regulators, not just to the cost line.
insights.quote: agentic AI reduced the end-to-end claim-processing time from between 30 to 60 minutes to between 2 to 4 minutes
insights.locator: How Agents Are Assisting One Insurer

insights.claim: About one-third of claims arriving in unstructured formats caused the bottlenecks, capacity overflows, and multi-week backlogs at the European insurer — the specific chokepoint agents removed.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Names the exact technical gap legacy automation could not close — unstructured intake share is the diagnostic to ask any payer about before believing its automation ceiling.
insights.quote: Manual processes were slowed by the cases that arrived in unstructured formats (about one-third of the total), creating persistent bottlenecks and capacity overflows that led to a backlog of several weeks.
insights.locator: How Agents Are Assisting One Insurer

insights.claim: Embedding fraud-detection agents inside the same claims workflow let the European insurer cut claims leakage by 3% to 5% of total payout across the portfolio.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Leakage reduction hits the medical cost line, not admin expense — a far larger denominator, so 3%–5% of payout dwarfs typical back-office savings and should be modeled separately.
insights.quote: Across the portfolio, the insurer reduced claims leakage by 3% to 5% of total payout.
insights.locator: How Agents Are Assisting One Insurer

insights.claim: Once built, the same agentic AI architecture could be reused across other insurer processes with significantly reduced incremental effort for adaptation.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Implies declining marginal cost per automated process — first-mover investment amortizes, so early adopters' ROI accelerates while late entrants pay full freight on each build.
insights.locator: Moreover, once built, the same AI architecture could be reused

insights.claim: Claims cost management today targets waste, fraud, and abuse rather than prevention and ideal patient pathways, leaving the larger prevention lever largely untouched by the industry.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Positions prevention-led cost management as an under-exploited profit pool — payers that redeploy freed capacity there could out-earn peers stuck optimizing fraud recovery.
insights.quote: Claims cost management today is focused on waste, fraud, and abuse rather than on prevention and developing ideal patient pathways.
insights.locator: The news is not all negative

insights.claim: BCG research finds two-thirds of patients want personalized support including decision assistance with medical questions and day-to-day healthy-living advice, and client work has produced customer retention increases of as much as 14 percentage points and up to 70% reductions in claims costs.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: A 14-point retention swing plus outsized claims-cost reduction is the differentiation prize — watch payer retention and medical loss ratio disclosures for evidence anyone is capturing it.
insights.quote: customer retention increases of as much as 14 percentage points and up to 70% reductions in claims costs
insights.locator: Our client experience has shown big benefits

insights.claim: The end state is a shift from a rule-compliant processing factory to a personalized health partner, where the insurer moves from reactive cost reimbursor to active health partner funded by freed capacity and richer data from automated processes.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Reframes payer AI as a business-model change with revenue and retention upside, not a cost program — the valuation multiple implication is different.
insights.quote: The result is a fundamental shift from a rule-compliant processing factory to a personalized health partner.
insights.locator: Agents to the Rescue

insights.claim: Members receiving active case support from a dedicated contact who understands their full clinical history show significantly higher treatment adherence and lower downstream claims costs.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Links service investment directly to medical cost reduction, meaning personalization spend can be underwritten against MLR rather than treated as pure marketing expense.
insights.locator: Personalized Member Engagement

insights.claim: In the agentic service model the agent ranks members by urgency, complexity, and intervention potential, compiles a 360-degree overview before each interaction, proposes next-best actions in real time, and handles documentation afterwards — leaving the human only the conversation.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Concrete blueprint for what agent-augmented service actually looks like; the ranking-plus-briefing layer is where software vendors can insert themselves into payer workflows.
insights.locator: Regardless of member health status, agents facilitate the service

themes.theme: Governance, regulation, and the human layer

insights.claim: Governance will settle into one of two modes — full supervision where every decision is reviewed by a human specialist before leaving the organization, or strategic oversight with performance monitoring, quality sampling, and rule maintenance — chosen per process by regulation and internal risk appetite.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: The governance mode chosen determines how much of the theoretical automation ceiling actually converts to savings — full supervision keeps the human cost in place.
insights.locator: Companies will organize governance in one of two ways

insights.claim: Experienced payer staff shift from transaction processing into governing the agentic system itself — updating rule sets, monitoring decision quality, detecting accuracy 'drift', and managing regulatory documentation — alongside handling complex appeals and novel fraud patterns.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Creates persistent demand for AI observability, drift monitoring, and audit tooling inside regulated payers — a durable software category rather than a one-off implementation.
insights.locator: Specialists and AI Governors

insights.claim: In stringently regulated markets many claims and eligibility processes qualify as high-risk AI under emerging frameworks such as the EU's AI Act, so governance, auditability, and documentation must be integrated from day one.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Regulatory classification is a gating cost that advantages incumbents with compliance muscle and platform architectures over point-solution startups in EU payer markets.
insights.locator: Regulatory Readiness

insights.claim: Insurers should engage regulators preemptively at the level of platform-level design decisions rather than presenting individual use cases, highlighting risks and built-in mitigations early.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: A non-obvious regulatory strategy: approving an architecture once beats re-litigating every use case, which compounds speed advantage for platform-first adopters.
insights.quote: Don’t think about individual use cases and involve regulators early in platform-level design decisions.
insights.locator: Regulatory Readiness

insights.claim: New payer job categories will emerge — AI operations specialists designing agentic workflows, process quality governors managing accuracy and absence of AI bias, and human-AI interaction designers building interfaces for governors and customer-facing AI call agents.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Job-posting counts in these three categories are a leading indicator of which payers are actually past the pilot stage.
insights.locator: New roles for human staff will also emerge

insights.claim: Success in large-scale AI transformation follows a 10-20-70 rule: roughly 10% of the work is in AI applications and algorithms, 20% in technology and data, and 70% in people, organization, and processes.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: If 70% of the value depends on organizational change, model quality is not the differentiator — bet on execution capability and change-management track record, not on who has the best LLM.
insights.quote: success follows what we call the 10-20-70 rule: roughly 10% of the work lies in AI applications and algorithms, 20% in technology and data, and 70% in people, organization, and processes
insights.locator: How to Get It Right

insights.claim: Insurers should choose a composable, platform-based architecture over individual point solutions — accepting higher initial investment in exchange for full control, reduced single-vendor dependence, and replicability across processes and partnerships.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Explicit anti-lock-in advice to buyers is a headwind for single-vendor payer AI suites and a tailwind for modular infrastructure players.
insights.locator: Architecture. Choose a composable, platform-based approach

insights.claim: The right lighthouse projects are processes with high manual intensity, clear rules, and high reusability — claims reimbursement and enrollment are near-universal strong starting points that generate quick proof points and internal acceptance.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Reusability, not just savings size, is the selection criterion — a filter for judging whether a company's first AI project builds compounding capability or a dead end.
insights.locator: Lighthouse Examples

insights.claim: Early movers in agentic health insurance are already compounding their advantage and the gap to followers is widening, so late adopters will not be locked out but will pay more, progress slower, and chase a moving target.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Argues for dispersion within the payer sector rather than a rising tide — pair-trade leaders against laggards on evidence of process-level (not tool-level) deployment.
insights.quote: Late adopters won’t be locked out, but they will pay more, make slower progress, and find themselves playing catch-up with a moving target.
insights.locator: Agentic AI in health insurance is no longer experimental

insights.claim: The winners will not be the organizations that automate the most but those that best redirect human expertise to where it creates irreplaceable value, meaning agentic AI is deployed to reallocate rather than cut headcount.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/konstantin-storms
insights.so_what: Cuts against the pure cost-cutting AI narrative — implies payer savings show up more slowly and partly as revenue/retention, so headcount-based AI models may misprice the effect.
insights.quote: The organizations that succeed won’t be those that automate the most but those that best redirect human expertise to where it creates irreplaceable value.
insights.locator: The key to success: design for humans from the start
